introduction: “Whatsoever preventeth you from God is an idol, even were it to be of the highest existence.” Bahá’u’lláh takes the prophets’ war on idols and turns it inward. The idols He means are desires, “idle fancies,” inherited beliefs, revered names and persons, anything a mind sets up and then bows to; the people He addresses were strict monotheists who thought idolatry a sin of others. Abraham, who broke his father’s images, is the model, and the golden calf the standing example. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds the philosophical point that any God a mind can picture is its own product, and distinguishes a keepsake from an object of homage. The Hebrew prophets’ satires on the idol-maker, the Qur’án’s Abraham, and Paul’s “covetousness, which is idolatry” lie behind the readings and are quoted beside them; Bacon’s “idols of the mind” carries the idea into science. Some readings speak sharply of the images of India and of Christian churches. Vivekananda’s reply at Chicago, the Rig Veda’s “many names,” Ibn ‘Arabí’s heart “capable of every form,” and Carlyle’s doubt that anyone ever took an image for God are set beside them so that the question can be heard from the other side.
questions: “Whatsoever preventeth you from God is an idol.” By that definition, what are the idols of an educated person today? What are yours?
“They worship names and perceive it not.” What is the difference between honouring a name and worshipping it?
A photograph for memory’s sake is harmless; “extraordinary homage” is idolatry. Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent Moses had made. When does a symbol stop helping and start standing in the way?
Vivekananda calls images “pegs to hang the spiritual ideas on.” How would you state the disagreement between him and these readings fairly to both?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that a God imagined by the mind is the mind’s own product. How, on that view, is God to be known at all?

outside.why: “Whatsoever preventeth you from God is an idol, even were it to be of the highest existence.” John ends a letter about love with a single warning: little children, keep yourselves from idols.
An idol need not be an image. Jesus: no man can serve two masters. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
“The idols are your vain desires.” The Qur’án: hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god?
Paul names one such desire outright, in a list of things to be put to death in oneself: covetousness, which is idolatry.

“Be not of those who fashion idols with their own hands and then bow down before the work of their own making.” Isaiah watches a man cut a tree, warm himself and cook with part of it: and the residue thereof he maketh a god; he falleth down unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
Abraham in the Qur’án: worship ye that which ye yourselves do carve?
“They worship names and perceive it not.” The Qur’án: they are but names which ye have named, ye and your fathers, for which Allah hath revealed no warrant.

Bacon carried the word into philosophy: there are four classes of Idols which beset men’s minds: Idols of the Tribe, of the Cave, of the Market-place, of the Theatre. The third are the idols of words.
“They have clung to the idols of their own” selves. The psalm on what an idol does to its maker: they that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.
Some “make for themselves an imaginary God and adore this.” Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen.

Feuerbach said that the same is true of every God men worship: the true sense of Theology is Anthropology. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá agrees that “whatever fits in the mind is merely imagined.” What does he say can be known, and how, that keeps the argument from ending where Feuerbach’s does?
One worships the sun, another trees and stones. Paul at Athens: we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device.
Paul: who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.

“Imaginary gods are superstitious phantoms.” Jeremiah on the decked and gilded image: they are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them.

A photograph kept “for memory’s sake” does no harm; “extraordinary homage” to it is idolatry. King Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent Moses himself had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it.

Carlyle doubted that anyone ever worshipped the object: Idol is Eidolon, a thing seen, a symbol. It is not God, but a Symbol of God; and perhaps one may question whether any the most benighted mortal ever took it for more than a Symbol. If he is right, where does the wrong in idolatry lie?
When husband or wife “adores the other instead of God,” each bars the other’s way. Jesus: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.

Abraham turned out an old guest who would not name God, and was rebuked. Franklin retold the story as a new chapter of Genesis: have I borne with him these hundred ninety and eight years, and couldst not thou, that art thyself a sinner, bear with him one night?
Many worship idols “while imagining” they believe in God. Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord.
“They make mention of God with their tongues while their hearts tell of images.” Isaiah: with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.
“Names for which God hath given no authority.” The Qur’án on persons put in God’s place: they have taken as lords beside Allah their rabbis and their monks.
“Have ye turned to temples made by the hands of Our servants while setting aside the Temple of God?” Paul: God dwelleth not in temples made with hands.
Asked for evidence, they say they found it so among their fathers. The Qur’án: we follow that wherein we found our fathers. What! Even though their fathers were wholly unintelligent?
“Break the idols of vain imitation.” Abraham began with his own father: takest thou idols for gods? Lo! I see thee and thy folk in error manifest.
“Do ye worship the calf and forsake Him Who created you?” Sinai, forty days after the commandments: he made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel.
Jeroboam is named as the founder of idol worship in Israel. Kings: the king made two calves of gold, and said, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel.
Ignorance led people to worship the sun. Moses: lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, shouldest be driven to worship them.
To worship “stony forms which are devoid of spirit” when God has given reason. Habakkuk: woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach!

The images of India are called “superstitions and imaginations.” Swami Vivekananda answered that charge in Chicago in 1893: the images, crosses, and crescents are simply so many symbols, so many pegs to hang the spiritual ideas on. What would each speaker need to grant the other?
The oldest Indian scripture on its many gods: to what is One, sages give many a title. How does a tradition tell the difference between many names for the One and many gods?

The likeness of the Buddha is worshipped by millions; “what benefit does he draw from this?” The Buddha asked for no such thing: don’t go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by the thought, This contemplative is our teacher.

Images, candles and bells in churches are traced to pagan usage. Ibn ‘Arabí looked on every form of worship more gently: my heart has become capable of every form: it is a convent for Christian monks, and a temple for idols, and the pilgrim’s Ka‘ba. Is his breadth a failure to see the danger, or a way past it?
They answer the sound of brass and “deprive their ears of the divine call.” Paul: I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
Earlier peoples “each day took a different god.” Joshua reminds Israel of its own beginnings: your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, and they served other gods.
“Every soul hath taken unto himself an idol besides God.” The first commandment: thou shalt have no other gods before me.
“If ye seek other than Me, it is but an idol unto you.” The psalmist: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
“Shatter the idols of vain imaginings.” Paul: ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
“When the Friend … turned toward the abode of the idols.” The Qur’án: then he reduced them to fragments, all save the chief of them, that haply they might have recourse to it.
“The Abraham of faith.” Abraham’s own way out of idolatry in the Qur’án: when it set, he said: I love not things that set.
“Though thou art a woman, arise … and break the deity of idle imagination with the might of Abraham.” Elijah on Carmel: if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.

One who “recognized Him in days when all turned away … and took idols.” Three men before a king’s image: be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
“I have not worshipped and will never worship any but God.” The chapter of the Qur’án this echoes ends: unto you your religion, and unto me my religion.

shortfall: Most of the 74 readings are single sentences that repeat one command (“shatter the idols of vain imaginings”) or one observation (people worship idols while supposing they worship God). The guide is read with 42 outside quotations, placed where they give a source, a parallel or an objection; none was added only to reach the number.

isaiah-the-residue-thereof-he-maketh-a-g.text: He burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh; he roasteth roast, and is satisfied: yea, he warmeth himself, and saith, Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire: And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god

exodus-these-be-thy-gods-o-israel.text: And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt

quran-takest-thou-idols-for-gods.text: (Remember) when Abraham said unto his father Azar: Takest thou idols for gods? Lo! I see thee and thy folk in error manifest.

john-epistle-keep-yourselves-from-idols.text: Little children, keep yourselves from idols

colossians-covetousness-which-is-idolatr.text: Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry

jeremiah-upright-as-the-palm-tree.text: For the customs of the people are vain: for one cutteth a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman, with the axe. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not. They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good

habakkuk-what-profiteth-the-graven-image.text: What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it

bacon-four-classes-of-idols.text: There are four classes of Idols which beset men’s minds. To these for distinction’s sake I have assigned names,—calling the first class Idols of the Tribe; the second, Idols of the Cave; the third, Idols of the Market-place; the fourth, Idols of the Theatre
bacon-four-classes-of-idols.author: Francis Bacon
